Surah An-Naml (The Ant)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾. Its clarification has already been given, with Qur'anic verses, at the beginning of Surah "Al-Baqarah," in the discussion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Guidance for those who are mindful of God﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 2].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When Moses said to his family, "Indeed, I have perceived a fire"﴾ — and to the end of the story. Its explanation has already preceded in Surah Maryam (Mary), Surah Taha, and Surah al-A'raf.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Solomon inherited from David﴾. We have already mentioned that it is an inheritance of knowledge and religion, not an inheritance of wealth, in surah Maryam, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾ [Maryam: 5-6]. And we explained there the evidences that the prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, do not have their wealth inherited from them.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 25 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Not to prostrate before Allah, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you disclose.﴾ Its explanation has already been given, with Qur'anic evidence, at the beginning of Surah "Hud", in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Verily they fold their breasts to hide from Him. Yet when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they keep secret and what they disclose. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾ [Hud: 5]. As for His saying ﴿not to prostrate before Allah﴾:
• It is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allah, who created them, if it is Him that you worship.﴾ [Fussilat: 37]
• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him].﴾ [al-Najm: 62]. His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿who brings forth the hidden (al-khab')﴾. Some scholars said: al-khab' in the heavens is the rain, and al-khab' in the earth is the plants, the minerals and the treasures, and this meaning suits His saying: ﴿who brings forth the hidden (al-khab')﴾. Other scholars said: al-khab' is the secret and the unseen, meaning: (p-110) He knows what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, as is indicated by His saying after it: ﴿and knows what you conceal and what you disclose.﴾
• And like His saying in this noble surah: ﴿And there is no unseen thing in the heaven or the earth but that it is in a clear Record.﴾ [al-Naml: 75]
• And His saying: ﴿And not absent from your Lord is an atom's weight within the earth or within the heaven, nor anything smaller than that or greater, but that it is in a clear Record.﴾ [Yunus: 61], as we have clarified in Surah "Hud".

The majority of the Seven readers, other than al-Kisa'i, read this word ﴿ألّا يَسْجُدُوا لِلَّهِ﴾ with the lam of the word "alla" (ألّا) doubled (shaddah). There is no disagreement on this reading that "yasjudu" (يَسْجُدُوا) is a present-tense verb in the subjunctive, governed by "an" (أنْ) assimilated into "la" (لا). The present-tense verb on this reading, together with the verbal "an" assimilated into "la", forms a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of an accusative, according to the more apparent view, and it was said it is in the position of a genitive. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) has several possibilities:

The first: It is accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), meaning: ﴿And Satan made their deeds seem good to them﴾, for the sake of ﴿not prostrating to Allah﴾, that is, for the sake of their not prostrating to Allah; or ﴿so he averted them from the way﴾, for the sake of ﴿not prostrating to Allah﴾. al-Akhfash said the first, and al-Kisa'i said the second.

al-Yazidi and others said: it is accusative as a substitute (badal) for "a'malahum" (their deeds), meaning: ﴿And Satan made their deeds seem good to them: not to prostrate﴾, that is, their not prostrating. On this view, their deeds are their not prostrating to Allah, and this analysis indicates that abandonment is an action, as we have clarified in Surah "al-Furqan", in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Messenger says: "My Lord, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned."﴾ [al-Furqan: 30].

Some of them said: the verbal noun mentioned is in the position of a genitive, as a substitute (badal) for "al-sabil" (the way), or because the governing element in it is ﴿so they are not guided﴾. On these two views the word "la" (لا) is extra (silah). On the first of these two, the meaning is: ﴿so he averted them from the way﴾ of their prostrating to Allah, and on this view the path of truth from which they were averted is prostrating to Allah, and "la" is an emphatic extra particle. On the second, the meaning is: ﴿so they are not guided﴾, because [they do not prostrate] to Allah, that is, to prostrating to Him, and "la" is also an extra emphatic particle.

It is known in the science of Arabic grammar that when the verbal noun formed from a verb and a literal relative particle is negated, the word "adam" (عَدَمُ, absence) is mentioned before the verbal noun, so that the meaning of the negation governing the verb is conveyed by it. So your saying, for example: "I wondered that you do not stand" (عَجِبْتُ مِن أنْ لا تَقُومَ), when you form its verbal noun, requires you to say: "I wondered at the absence of your standing" (عَجِبْتُ مِن عَدَمِ قِيامِكَ). When the verb is affirmative, you do not mention the word "adam" with the verbal noun; if you say "I wondered that you stand" (عَجِبْتُ مِن أنْ تَقُومَ), then in forming its verbal noun you say: "I wondered at your standing" (عَجِبْتُ مِن قِيامِكَ), as is not hidden. Accordingly, the verbal noun (p-111) formed from His saying ﴿alla yasjudu﴾ must be expressed as "the absence of prostration", unless "la" is considered an extra particle. We have indicated in Surah "al-A'raf", in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], that we explained the discussion of the extra "la" for emphasis of speech in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab", at the beginning of Surah "al-Balad", in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I swear not by this city﴾ [al-Balad: 1].

We will mention here a portion of what we said on this. We said: The first view, and the majority hold it, is that "la" here is an extra particle according to the custom of the Arabs, for they sometimes utter the word "la" without intending its original meaning, but merely to strengthen and emphasise the speech. Like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray,﴾ ﴿from following me?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92-93], meaning: "from following me". And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾, meaning: "from prostrating", according to one of the two views. This is supported by His saying in Surah "Sad": ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾ [Sad: 75]. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So that the People of the Scripture may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29]. And His saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾ (the verse) [al-Nisa': 65], meaning: "by your Lord". And His saying: ﴿And not equal are the good deed and the bad deed﴾ [Fussilat: 34], meaning: "and the bad deed". And His saying: ﴿And there is a prohibition upon a city which We have destroyed, that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya': 95], according to one of the two views. And His saying: ﴿And what will make you know that when it comes they will not believe?﴾ [al-An'am: 109], according to one of the two views. And His saying: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite what your Lord has prohibited to you: that you associate nothing with Him"﴾ (the verse) [al-An'am: 151], according to one of the previously mentioned views; and like the saying of Abu al-Najm:

"So I do not blame the fair ones for not mocking (alla taskhara)
what they saw of the white-haired, withered old man."

meaning: "that they mock". And the saying of another:

"And you rebuke me in amusement, that I not love it (alla uhibbahu),
while for amusement there is a constant caller, never unaware."

meaning: "that I love it", and "la" is extra. And the saying of another:

"His generosity refused, not stinginess, and it was hastened with him,
yes, from a youth who does not prevent hunger from killing him."

meaning: "His generosity refused stinginess", and "la" is extra, though there is disagreement about its extra use in this last verse, especially on the narration with "al-bukhl" in the genitive, because "la" then governs what is a noun meaning the particle "la", so it is not extra on the genitive narration. And the saying of Imru' al-Qais: (p-112)

"So no, by your father, daughter of the Amiri, (fala wa-abikiya)
the people do not claim that I flee."

meaning: "and by your father", and al-Farra' cited, as evidence for the extra use of "la" in speech that carries the sense of denial, the saying of the poet:

"The Messenger of Allah was not pleased with their religion,
and the two best men, Abu Bakr and 'Umar."

meaning: "'Umar", and "la" is extra. al-Jawhari cited for its extra use the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

"In a pit of destruction he travelled, and did not perceive
his falsehood until he saw the dawn appear."

Al-Hur means destruction, meaning: "in a pit of destruction", and "la" is extra, as said by Abu 'Ubayda and others. al-Asma'i cited for its extra use the saying of Sa'ida al-Hudhali:

"Is it from you, [the lightning], that there was a flash whose glimmer
vanished, its peak, the blaze of a sparkling flame?"

It is narrated: "Afa-minka" and "tashayyumuhu" in place of "Afa-anka" and "tasannumuhu", meaning: "Is it from you that there was lightning", and "la" is extra. Among the evidences of its extra use is the saying of a poet:

"I remembered Layla, and passion overtook me,
and the core of my heart nearly did not break apart."

meaning: "nearly broke apart". As for Abu 'Ubayda's use of the extra "la" as evidence, citing the saying of al-Shammakh:

"O 'A'isha, what is the matter with your people, that I do not see them
wasting the noble camels along with the wasteful one?"

this is an error on his part, for "la" in the verse of al-Shammakh here is negating, not extra, and his intended meaning is that she forbids him from guarding his wealth, while her own people guard their wealth; that is: I do not see your people wasting their wealth while you rebuke me for guarding my wealth. As for what al-Farra' mentioned, that the word "la" is extra only in speech that carries the sense of denial, this is a general rule that does not hold absolutely, by the evidence of some of the examples mentioned earlier that contain no denial, like this verse on the view that "la" in it is extra, and like the verse of Sa'ida al-Hudhali. And as for what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that "la" is extra only at the beginning of speech and nowhere else, there is no evidence for it. The purpose of our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" ends here.

This word is read by al-Kisa'i alone among the Seven: ﴿Alla yasjudu﴾ with the lam of the word "alla" (ألا) lightened (not doubled). On al-Kisa'i's reading, the word "alla" (ألا) is an interjection of opening and attention, and "ya" (يا) is the particle of address, and the one addressed is omitted, its estimate being: "Alā yā hā'ulā'i-s-judū" (ألا يا هَؤُلاءِ اسْجُدُوا), "O you, prostrate". "Usjudu" (اسْجُدُوا) is an imperative verb. It is known in the science of readings that if you are told to stop at each word separately in al-Kisa'i's reading, you stop at His saying ﴿alla yasjudu﴾ three times. The first: you stop on "alā". The second: you stop on "yā". The third: you stop on "usjudū". This is a stop for testing (waqf ikhtibar), not a stop of choice (waqf ikhtiyar). As for the reading of the majority, you stop only twice: the first on "alla" (ألّا), and you do not stop on "an" because it is assimilated into "la"; the second, you stop on "yasjudū".

Know that on al-Kisa'i's reading, two alifs have been omitted in the written script: the first is the alif attached to the vocative particle "yā", and the second is the alif of connection (alif al-wasl) in His saying "usjudū" (اسْجُدُوا). Some scholars explained the omission of these two in the script by saying: since they are dropped in pronunciation, they are dropped in writing. They said: there is much of this in the Qur'an.

Know that the majority of the scholars hold, as we have mentioned on al-Kisa'i's reading, that the word "alā" (ألا) is for opening and attention, that "yā" is a particle of address from which the alif is omitted in the script, and that "usjudū" is an imperative verb. They said: omitting the one addressed while mentioning the vocative particle is a well-known Arabic style, and from it is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"Alā yā-slamī yā Hind, Hind of the Banu Bakr,
even if they were our enemies until the end of time."

And the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"Alā yā-slamī yā dar Mayya, upon the desolation,
and may rain never cease to pour upon your sandy ground."

So his saying in the two verses "alā yā-slamī" means: "O you, be safe, O woman". And the saying of another:

"Yā-slamī, Dhāt al-Damālīj wa-l-'Iqd" [O be safe, you who wear the bracelets and the necklace]

And the saying of al-Shammakh:

"Alā yā-ṣbaḥānī before the raid of Sinjal,
and before deaths have come and my term has come."

meaning: "Alā yā ṣaḥbī-ṣbaḥānī", "O my companions, greet me with morning". Its parallel is the saying of another:

"Alā yā-sqiyānī before the horses of Abu Bakr."

And from it is the saying of another: (p-114)

"She said: 'Alā yā-smaʿ, I will admonish you with a sermon,'
so I said: 'We hear, speak and make your point.'"

meaning: "Alā yā hadhā-smaʿ", "O this one, listen". Sibawayh cited, for omitting the one addressed while mentioning the vocative particle, the saying of a poet:

"Yā la'natu-llāhi wa-l-aqwāmi kulli-him
wa-ṣ-ṣāliḥīna ʿalā Samʿāna min jār"

with the "t" of "la'nat" [lāʿnatu] in "la'natu Allāh" vowelled with a damma; then he said: "fa-yā la-ghayr al-la'na" (then, O not the curse), meaning that the intended is: "O people, the curse of Allah...", to the end. The author of al-Lisan cited, for omitting the one addressed while mentioning the vocative particle, as evidence for al-Kisa'i's reading mentioned, the saying of a poet:

"Yā qātala-llāhu ṣibyānan tajī'u bihim
Umm al-Hunaynayni min Zandalihā Wārā"

then he said: "It is as if he intended: 'O people, may Allah kill the children...'", and the saying of another:

"Yā man ra'ā bāriqan ukaffikfuhu
bayna dhirāʿay wa-jabhat al-asad"

then he said: "It is as if he called: 'O people, O my brothers,' and when they turned to him he said: 'Man ra'a' (who saw)". Some cited, for omitting the one addressed while mentioning the vocative particle, the saying of ʿAntara in his Mu'allaqa:

"Yā shāta mā qanaṣin li-man ḥallat lahu
ḥarumat ʿalayya wa-laytahā lam taḥrimi"

They said: the estimate is: "O people, look at the ewe of the hunt..."

Know that a group of scholars said: "Ya" in the reading of al-Kisa'i, and in all the examples we have mentioned, is not for calling (nida'), but is for alerting (tanbih). So each of alla and ya is an interjection of alerting, repeated for emphasis. Among those reported as holding this view is Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur, and this view was chosen by Abu Hayyan in "al-Bahr al-Muhit," where he said: "What I incline to is that this kind of construction reported from the Arabs does not have ya in it for calling, and the one called upon has been omitted. For in my view the one called upon cannot be omitted, because the verb that governs the calling has been omitted, and its subject has been dropped along with it. If the one called upon were omitted, that would involve omitting the whole calling clause and omitting its complement, which is the one called upon, and that would be a great deficiency. And if we leave the one called upon and do not omit it, that is evidence of the governing element in it, namely the calling clause. The particle of calling is not a particle of response like na'am, la, bala, and ajal, after which clauses may be omitted because the preceding question indicates the omitted clauses. So ya in my view in those constructions is an interjection of alerting with which alla, which is itself for alerting, is emphasized, and this is permissible because the two particles differ and for the purpose of intensifying emphasis. Since emphasis has been found in the combination of two particles that differ in form and are both governing, as in his saying: 'Fa-asbahna la yas'alnani 'an bima bihi' (p-115), and the two that agree in form and are both governing, as in his saying: 'Wa la lalamma bihim abadan dawa'," and this is permissible even if they count it as a necessity (darura) or rare. The combination of non-governing particles that differ in form is permissible, and ya in his saying: 'Ya la'nata Allahi wal-aqwami kulihim' is not, in my view, a particle of calling, but a particle of alerting followed by the subject (mubtada'), and it is not one from which the one called upon has been omitted, for the reason we have stated." End of Abu Hayyan's words, and what he chose has a basis in reasoning.

His commentator (muqayyid) said, may Allah pardon him and forgive him: Among what has a basis in reasoning in my view regarding al-Kisa'i's reading is that his saying "ya-asjudu" is a present-tense verb from which the nun of the nominative (nun al-raf') has been dropped, without any governing particle, jussive particle, emphatic nun, or protective nun (nun al-wiqaya).

Some scholars have said that dropping it without any of the stated reasons is a sound dialect (lugha sahiha).

Al-Nawawi said in "Sharh Muslim," in the seventeenth part, on page 702, the following text: His saying: "O Messenger of Allah, how will they hear and how will they respond when they have decayed?" Thus it is in most copies: "kayfa yasma'u" and "wa-anna yujibu" without a nun, and this is a sound dialect, though rarely used, and its explanation has preceded several times. Among them is the hadith previously mentioned in "Iman": "You will not enter Paradise until you believe," end of quotation from him. Since dropping the nun of the nominative is a sound dialect, there is no objection to his words, may He be exalted, "yasjudu" in the reading of al-Kisa'i being a present-tense verb. And there is no doubt that this has a basis in reasoning. We limited ourselves in Surat al-Hijr to the point that its dropping is restricted to what is heard (al-sama'), and we mentioned some of its examples. And Allah knows best.

* *

Two notes.

The first: Know that the verified position is that this verse of "al-Naml" is a place of prostration (sajda) according to both readings, because al-Kisa'i's reading contains the command to prostrate, and the reading of the majority contains the blame and rebuke of one who abandons prostration. By this you know that the view of al-Zajjaj and those who agree with him, that it is not a place of prostration according to the reading of the majority, but is a place of prostration only according to al-Kisa'i's reading, is contrary to what is verified. Al-Zamakhshari and others have drawn attention to this.

* *

The second note: Know that according to the reading of the majority, it is not good to pause at His saying "la yahtadun" (they are not guided), while according to al-Kisa'i's reading, it is good to pause there.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: "Wa ya'lamu ma tukhfuna wa ma tu'linun" (and He knows what you conceal and what you disclose), Hafs and al-Kisa'i read it with the second-person ta' (taa' fawqiyya), addressing directly, while the rest read "yukhfuna" and "yu'linun" with the third-person ya' (taa' tahtiyya). And Allah knows best.

(Commentary of al-Shinqiti, Adwa' al-Bayan)

In the book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" the author said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah An-Naml (The Ant)

His statement, exalted is He, reporting about Bilqis: ﴿And indeed, I am going to send them a gift and will wait to see what the envoys will return with.﴾

This indicates that she sent multiple envoys to Sulayman. And His statement: ﴿So when [the envoy] came to Sulayman﴾ [An-Naml: 36], with the singular form of the verb "jaa'a" (came), and His statement, exalted is He, reporting about Sulayman that he said: ﴿Return to them, for we will surely come to them with soldiers﴾ [An-Naml: 37], and so on, indicates that the messenger was one.

The apparent answer, as mentioned by more than one scholar, is that the messengers were a group, and there was a leader among them. So the plural refers to all of them, and the singular refers to the leader, because those with him are followers of him. And Allah knows best.

**Allah's words: ﴿And whoever gives thanks, he gives thanks only for the benefit of himself﴾.** Its meaning is made clear in several other verses:

• As in His words: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul﴾ [Fussilat: 46]

• And His words: ﴿And whoever does righteousness, they are preparing for themselves﴾ [al-Rum: 44]

• And His words: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls﴾ [al-Isra': 7].

**Allah's words: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, indeed my Lord is Free of need, Generous﴾.** Its meaning is also made clear in many verses, such as His words: ﴿And Musa said: If you disbelieve, you and whoever is on the earth entirely, indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾ [Ibrahim: 8]; and His words: ﴿But they disbelieved and turned away, and Allah was self-sufficient, and Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Taghabun: 6]; and His words: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor toward Allah, and Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Taghabun: 6]; and His words: ﴿And Allah is the Free of need, and you are the poor. And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people; then they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad: 38]; and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 45:

The Exalted said: ﴿And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah," but they became two factions contending with each other.﴾

In this noble verse, the Majestic and Exalted mentions that He sent His prophet Salih to Thamud. ﴿But they became two factions contending with each other.﴾ Here He does not explain the nature of the dispute between the two factions, but He does explain it in surah al-A'raf (tafsir: exegesis), in His saying: ﴿The eminent ones among his people who had been arrogant said to those who were oppressed—to those among them who had believed, "Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?" They said, "Indeed, we are believers in that with which he has been sent."﴾ ﴿Those who were arrogant said, "Indeed, we are, in that which you believe, disbelievers."﴾ [al-A'raf: 75–76]. This, then, is their dispute, and the greatest kind of dispute is the dispute over disbelief and faith.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 46:

(p-117) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "O my people, why do you seek to hasten the evil before the good?"﴾ We have already presented the verses that clarify this in surah "al-Ra'd" (Thunder), in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good, though exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6].

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 47:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "We have taken an omen from you and from those with you." He said, "Your omen is with Allah; rather, you are a people being tested."﴾ His saying, ﴿We have taken an omen from you﴾, meaning: we consider you a bad omen. When drought, calamity or misfortune befell the people of Salih, they would say: "This has come upon us only because of the ill omen of Salih and of those who believed in him." *Tatayyur* (taking omens of ill luck) means *tashaum* (considering something an ill omen), and its original derivation is from augury by observing the flight of birds.

We have already explained how omens of ill luck and good luck are taken from birds in Surah Al-An'am, in our discussion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾ [Al-An'am: 59], and His saying: ﴿Your omen is with Allah﴾. Some of the scholars said: that is, your cause, from which your good and your evil come, is with Allah. So the evil that befell you is due to your sins, not to the ill omen of Salih and of those among his people who believed in him.

We have also previously explained the meaning of *ta'ir al-insan* (a person's omen) in Surah Bani Isra'il, in our discussion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck﴾ [Al-Isra': 13]. What this noble verse indicates of the disbelievers' considering Salih and those with him among the believers an ill omen has a similar parallel, made clear in other verses of the Book of Allah. Such as His saying, Exalted is He, about the ill omen Pharaoh and his people took from Musa: ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours," and if evil afflicted them, they took an omen from Musa and those with him. Is not their omen with Allah? But most of them do not know﴾ [Al-A'raf: 131]. And His saying, Exalted is He, about the disbelievers of Quraysh taking omens from our Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And if good comes to them, they say, "This is from Allah," and if evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you." Say: "All is from Allah." So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any word?﴾ [An-Nisa': 78]. The "good" in both verses means blessings such as provision, plenty and well-being, and the "evil" means calamity through barrenness and drought, loss of wealth, lives and fruits. Also His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have taken an omen from you. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and a painful punishment will surely touch you."﴾ ﴿They said, "Your omen is with you."﴾ [Ya-Sin: 18-19]. That is, your affliction came to you from your sins and your disbelief.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾, some of the scholars said: (p-118) you are being examined. Others said: you are being punished, as in His saying: ﴿On the day they will be tried over the Fire﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 13]. We have already mentioned that the original meaning of *fitnah* (trial) in the language is placing gold in fire to test by smelting whether it is counterfeit or pure. And that it is used in the Qur'an with four meanings:

The first: its use for burning with fire, as in His saying: ﴿On the day they will be tried over the Fire﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 13], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who tormented the believing men and believing women﴾ [Al-Buruj: 10], meaning: they burned them in the fire of the trench, according to one of the two interpretations, which some verifying scholars have chosen.

The second meaning: the use of *fitnah* for testing, and this is its most frequent usage, as in His saying: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 35], and His saying: ﴿Had they remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink, that We might test them therein﴾ [Al-Jinn: 16-17]. Verses of this kind are numerous.

The third: the use of *fitnah* for the outcome of testing when that outcome is specifically evil. From this, *fitnah* was applied to disbelief and misguidance, as in His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 193], meaning: until no polytheism remains. This is the correct interpretation, as indicated by the Book and the Sunnah.

As for the Book: it is indicated by His saying after it in Al-Baqarah: ﴿And religion is for Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 193], and in Al-Anfal: ﴿And religion is entirely for Allah﴾ [Al-Anfal: 39]. This clarifies that the meaning of ﴿there is no fitnah﴾ is: no polytheism remains, because religion cannot be entirely for Allah as long as polytheism remains on earth, as you see.

As for the Sunnah: it is in his (ﷺ) saying: "I have been commanded to fight people until they testify that there is no god but Allah," and the hadith continues. He (ﷺ) made the goal at which his fighting of people ends the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is clear that the meaning of ﴿there is no fitnah﴾ is: no polytheism remains. So both the verse and the hadith indicate that the goal at which the fighting of the disbelievers ends is that no polytheism remain on earth. Yet He, in the verse, expressed this meaning by His saying: ﴿until there is no fitnah﴾, and he (ﷺ) expressed it by his saying: "until they testify that there is no god but Allah." So the goal in the verse and the hadith is one in meaning, as you see.

The fourth: the use of *fitnah* for proof (argument), in His saying: ﴿Then their fitnah (argument) was only that they said, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ (p-119) [Al-An'am: 23], meaning: their argument was not, as many have said. And knowledge is with Allah, Exalted is He.

The Qur'anic verse ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night, and then we will surely say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful.'"﴾ shows that the Prophet of Allah Salih, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, was helped by Allah through the support of his *waliyy* (heir), meaning his *awliya'* (protectors). This is because the word is in the construct form and is attached to a definite noun. The manner of their support for him is as follows. The nine men mentioned in Allah's words ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform﴾ ﴿They said, "Swear to one another"﴾ [an-Naml: 48–49] are those who, in the words "Swear to one another," that is, "make a pact by Allah," and in "We will surely attack him," that is, "we will surely assault him by night," so that "we will kill him and kill his family with him," and in "then we will surely say to his heir," that is, to his protectors and his kinsmen, and in "We did not witness the destruction of his family," that is, nor did we witness his own destruction. This indicates that they could not kill him openly, because of the support of his protectors for him, and their denial of having witnessed the destruction of his family is evidence of their fear of his protectors. The apparent meaning is that this support was a *'asabiyya nisbiyya* (tribal partisanship based on lineage), which has no connection to religion, and that his protectors were not Muslims.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this meaning in the commentary on Surah Hud, in the discussion of Allah's words ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed we see you as weak among us. And if not for your tribe, we would have stoned you"﴾ [Hud: 91], and in Surah Bani Isra'il, in the discussion of Allah's words ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra': 9]. As for Allah's words in this verse, ﴿Swear to one another﴾, the verified view is that it is an imperative verb (*fi'l amr*) reported by the word "they said." Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya permitted it to be a past-tense verb in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), but the first view is the correct one, if Allah wills, and Abu Hayyan attributed it to the majority of scholars. As for Allah's words in this verse, ﴿and indeed we are truthful﴾, the verified view concerning it is that they were lying in their statement ﴿and indeed we are truthful﴾, as is not hidden. By this you know that what al-Zamakhshari burdened himself with in *al-Kashshaf*, namely that they were truthful, has no basis, as Abu Hayyan pointed out and made clear.

The majority of the Seven Readers, other than Hamza and al-Kisa'i, read *la-nubayyitannahu* with a *nun* vowelled with a *damma* after the *lam*, and with a *fatha* on the second *ta'* that follows the first *ya'*. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *la-tubayyitunnahu* with a *ta'* vowelled with a *damma* after the *lam*, and with a *damma* on the *ta'* that follows the *ya'*. Also, the majority of the Seven Readers, other than Hamza and al-Kisa'i, read *thumma la-naqulannahu* with a *nun* vowelled with a *fatha* in place of the *ta'*, and with a *fatha* on the second *lam*. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *thumma la-taqulunnahu* with a *ta'* vowelled with a *fatha* after the first *lam*, and with a *damma* on the second *lam*. 'Asim read *mahlika ahlihi* with a *fatha* on the *mim*, and the others read it with a *damma*. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read *mahlika* with a *kasra* on the *lam*, and the others read it with a *fatha*.

The result is that Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read *mahlika* with a *fatha* on the *mim* and a *kasra* on the *lam*; that Abu Bakr, meaning Shu'ba, read on the authority of 'Asim *mahlaka* with a *fatha* on both the *mim* and the *lam*; and that others than 'Asim read *mahlika ahlihi* with a *damma* on the *mim* and a *fatha* on the *lam*. According to the reading of the one who reads *mahlika* with a *fatha* on the *mim*, it is a *masdar mimi* (a verbal noun formed with *mim*) from the triliteral *halaka*, and it may also be a noun of time or place (*ism zaman aw makan*). According to the reading of the one who reads *muhlaka* with a *damma* on the *mim*, it is also a *masdar mimi*, from the quadriliteral *ahlaka*, and it may likewise be a noun of time or place.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 51:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So look at what was the outcome of their plot: that We destroyed them and their people, all of them﴾ ﴿Those are their houses, empty because of what they wronged. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah﴾. In these noble verses, the Exalted has mentioned three matters:

The first: that He destroyed all of the people of Salih, and among them were the nine men (rahat) who used to spread corruption in the land and would not reform. This is in His saying: ﴿that We destroyed them and their people, all of them﴾, i.e., and they were the people of Salih, Thamud. ﴿Those are their houses, empty﴾, i.e., devoid of inhabitants because all of their people perished. ﴿because of what they wronged﴾, i.e., because of their wrongdoing, which was their disbelief, their rebellion, and their slaughter of the she-camel of Allah, which He had made a sign for them. Some of them said: ﴿empty﴾ means that its upper part had fallen upon its lower part.

The second: that the Exalted made their destruction, the people of Salih, a sign, i.e., a lesson by which those after them take warning, so that they beware of disbelief and of denying the messengers, lest there befall them what befell those people of destruction. This is in His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know﴾.

The third: that the Exalted saved those who believed and used to fear Allah from destruction and punishment, namely the Prophet of Allah Salih and those of his people who believed in him. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah﴾. These three matters that the Exalted mentioned here have been clarified in other verses.

As for His saving His prophet Salih and those who believed with him, and His destruction of Thamud, He clarified it in several places of His Book, such as His saying in Surat Hud: ﴿So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us and from the disgrace of that Day. Indeed your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty﴾ ﴿And those who wronged were seized by the blast, and they became in their homes prostrate dead﴾ ﴿as if they had never prospered there. Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud﴾ [Hud: 66-68]. This verse of Hud has also clarified the general destruction in this verse of An-Naml: the destruction mentioned in His saying: ﴿that We destroyed them and their people, all of them﴾, the verse of Hud has clarified that it was destruction by the blast, in His saying: ﴿And those who wronged were seized by the blast, and they became in their homes prostrate dead﴾ [Hud: 67], i.e., they were dead. As for His making their destruction a sign, He clarified it also in other places, such as His saying about them: ﴿So they hamstrung her and became regretful﴾ ﴿So the punishment seized them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 157-159]. And His saying in this noble verse: ﴿that We destroyed them and their people, all of them﴾ was read by Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir with a kasra on the hamza of inna (innā dammarnāhum), as a resumption (isti'naf). It was read by the Kufans, namely 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, as anna dammarnāhum with a fath on the hamza of anna. Regarding the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the verbal noun formed from anna and its clause according to the reading of the Kufans, there are several views. Among them: that it is a substitute (badal) for "the outcome of their plot"; and among them: that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being "it", i.e., "the outcome of their plot is Our destroying them."

These two views are, in my opinion, the closest of the views to the correct one, and therefore we have left aside the others. The pronoun in His saying "their plot" (makrihim) and in "We destroyed them" (dammarnahum) refers to the nine mentioned in His saying: ﴿And there were in the city nine men﴾, the verse [An-Naml: 48]. And His saying "empty" (khawiyah) is a circumstantial clause (hal) regarding "their houses", and its governing element is the indicative force contained in the meaning of "those" (tilka).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 54:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Do you commit an abomination while you see [it]?"﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Evil is the rain of those who were warned.﴾ We have already presented the verses in which the account of Lot and his people is clarified in Surat Hud, in the discussion of the story of Lot and his people. There we explained the statements of the people of knowledge (ahl al-ʿilm) and the discussion of their evidences regarding the punishment of the one who commits the abomination of sodomy (liwat). We also mentioned the verses that clarify it in Surat al-Hijr, in the discussion of the story of Lot and his people, and we mentioned some of that in Surat al-Furqan.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 60:

(p-122) And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is He who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow thereby gardens of delightful beauty...﴾. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is He who made the earth a stable resting place and placed within it rivers...﴾ [and the rest of the verses]. We have already explained the proofs for the resurrection contained in these verses at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah and the beginning of Surat al-Nahl.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah al-An'am, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾ [al-An'am: 59], and in other places.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 66:

The words of Allah the Most High: ﴿Nay, their knowledge has been completed concerning the Hereafter. Nay, they are in doubt about it. Nay, they are blind to it.﴾ The most apparent of the opinions of the people of knowledge concerning this noble verse, in my view, is that the meaning is: ﴿Nay, their knowledge has been completed﴾, i.e., their knowledge in the Hereafter has become complete when they witness it. That is, in the Hereafter they will know with complete knowledge what they used to be ignorant of in this world. As for His words: ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about it. Nay, they are blind to it﴾, i.e., in the abode of this world, this matter about which they used to doubt in the abode of this world, and which they were blind to regarding what the Messengers brought them, they will know in the Hereafter with complete knowledge that admits no doubt, upon witnessing what they used to deny of resurrection and recompense.

We have chosen this view over the other opinions of the exegetes concerning the verse because the Qur'an indicates it clearly in multiple verses; such as His words: ﴿Hear them and see them on the Day they come to Us! But the wrongdoers today are in manifest error﴾ [Maryam: 38]. His words: ﴿Hear them and see them on the Day they come to Us﴾ mean: how much they will hear and see the truth which they used to deny on the Day they come to Us, i.e., the Day of Resurrection. This clarifies the meaning of His words: ﴿Nay, their knowledge has been completed concerning the Hereafter﴾, i.e., their knowledge of it became complete because of their great intensity in hearing and seeing the truth at that time. His words: ﴿But the wrongdoers today are in manifest error﴾ [Maryam: 38] clarify the meaning of His words: ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about it. Nay, they are blind to it﴾, because their manifest error today, i.e., in the abode of this world, is their doubt about the Hereafter and their blindness to it. And like His words: ﴿So We have removed from you your covering, and today your sight is sharp﴾ [Qaf: 22], i.e., your knowledge today of what you used to deny in the world of what the Messengers brought you is sharp, i.e., strong and complete.

We have explained in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Illusion of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), in the surah of "al-Shura," in answering what is imagined as a contradiction between His words: ﴿They look with a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura: 45] and His words: ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾ [Qaf: 22], that the intended meaning of the sharpness of sight on that day is the completeness of knowledge and the strength of recognition. His words: ﴿If you could see when the criminals hang their heads before their Lord, [saying], "Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us [to the world] that we may do righteousness; indeed, we are [now] certain"﴾ [as-Sajdah: 12]. His words: ﴿indeed, we are [now] certain﴾, i.e., on the Day of Resurrection, clarify the meaning of His words here: ﴿Nay, their knowledge has been completed concerning the Hereafter﴾. And like His words: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows: "You have come to Us just as We created you the first time. But you claimed that We would not appoint for you an appointment."﴾ [al-Kahf: 48]. Their being presented before their Lord in rows is by it their knowledge is completed regarding what they used to deny. His words: ﴿But you claimed that We would not appoint for you an appointment﴾ are explicit that they were in doubt and blindness in the world regarding resurrection and recompense, as you see, along with other verses.

Know that His words "bal idarak" (بَلِ ادّارَكَ) have twelve readings, of which only two are Sab'i (canonical among the seven). Most of the Seven read it: بَلِ ادّارَكَ, with a kasrah on the lam of bal, and tashdid on the dal followed by an alif, and the alif before the dal is a hamzat wasl (connecting hamzah). Its origin is تَدارَكَ on the pattern تَفاعَلَ (tafa'ala). We have previously mentioned the reason for the idgham (assimilation) and the bringing in of the hamzat al-wasl in tafa'ala and tafa''ala, examples of that in the Qur'an, and some of its Arabic evidences, in the surah of "Ta-Ha," in the discussion of His words: ﴿Then suddenly it swallows what they fabricate﴾ [al-A'raf: 117]. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: بَلْ أدْرَكَ, with sukun on the lam of bal, a hamzat qat' (cutting hamzah) with fathah, and sukun on the dal, on the pattern أفْعَلَ (af'ala).

The meaning according to the reading of the majority: ﴿Nay, their knowledge has been completed (idarak)﴾, i.e., tadarak in the sense of takamal (became complete); like His words: ﴿Until, when they have all overtaken one another therein﴾ [al-A'raf: 38]. According to the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr: بَلْ أدْرَكَ (bal adraka), i.e., reached and attained.

Al-Baghawi said: i.e., it reached and attained, as one says: "adraka 'ilmi" when it reaches and attains him. The "idrab" (transition from one statement to another) in His words: ﴿Nay, their knowledge has been completed﴾, ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about it﴾, ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾, is an idrab intiqali (transitional). The apparent meaning is that "min" in His words: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾ means "'an" (concerning), and "'amun" is the plural of "'amin," which is the adjective from "'amiya, ya'ma," so he is "a'ma" and "'amm." From it is His words: ﴿Indeed, they were a blind people﴾ [al-A'raf: 64], and the words of Zuhayr in his Mu'allaqah:

"And I know the knowledge of today and of yesterday before it, but concerning the knowledge of what is in tomorrow I am blind."

This is the Qur'an that relates to the Children of Israel most of what they differ over. ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ.﴾

Among these differences is their dispute about Jesus. We have already mentioned in Surat Maryam (Chapter of Mary) their accusation against his mother of immorality, although a group among them believed in him, as His saying indicates: ﴿O you who believe, be helpers of Allah, as Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" The disciples said, "We are helpers of Allah." So a faction of the Children of Israel believed, and a faction disbelieved.﴾ [al-Saff: 41]. The group that believed spoke the truth about Jesus, while the group that disbelieved slandered him and his mother, as was already explained in Surat Maryam.

Allah has related to them in Surat Maryam, Surat al-Nisa' and elsewhere the reality of Jesus, son of Mary: that he is the servant of Allah [Maryam: 30] and His messenger, ﴿and His word which He directed to Maryam and a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 171]. When He explained to them the reality of his matter in detail in Surat Maryam, He said: ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary, the word of truth about which they dispute.﴾ [Maryam: 34]. This clarifies part of what His saying here indicates: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ.﴾

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 77:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, it is guidance and mercy for the believers﴾. We have already presented the verses that clarify this in the beginning of Surah "al-Kahf," in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] and so on.

The Exalted said: "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs and flee" (al-Naml 27:80).

Know that the verification indicated by the Qur'anic indications and by the inductive survey of the Qur'an is that the meaning of His saying, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear," admits, among the statements of the scholars, only two interpretations.

The first: the meaning is, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear," i.e., you cannot make the disbelievers hear, those whose hearts Allah has caused to die and for whom He has decreed wretchedness in His prior knowledge, the hearing of guidance and benefit. For Allah has decreed wretchedness upon them, so He sealed their hearts and their hearing, placed coverings over their hearts and deafness in their ears, (p-125) and a veil over their sight, so they do not hear the truth with the hearing of guidance and benefit. Among the Qur'anic indications that point to what we have mentioned is that after it He, exalted is He, said: "Nor can you guide the blind away from their error. You can make none hear except those who believe in Our signs" (al-Naml 27:81).

By this indication it becomes clear that the meaning of "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear" is: you cannot make those disbelievers, who are wretched in Allah's knowledge, hear with the hearing of guidance and acceptance of the truth. Their being opposed by Him, exalted is He, with the hearing negated in the verse concerning the dead, versus the hearing affirmed in it for those who believe in His signs, is a clear proof that what is meant by death in the verse is the death of disbelief and wretchedness, not the death of the soul's departure from the body. Had the meaning of death in His saying, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear," been the soul's departure from the body, He would not have contrasted His saying, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear," with His saying, "You can make none hear except those who believe in Our signs," but would have contrasted it with something suited to it, such as saying, "You can make none hear except those who have not died," i.e., whose souls have not departed their bodies, as is clear.

Since you know that this Qur'anic indication shows that what is meant by the dead here is the wretched, who do not hear the truth with the hearing of guidance and acceptance,

know that the inductive survey of the Great Qur'an points to this meaning, such as His saying, exalted is He: "Only those who hear respond; as for the dead, Allah will raise them, then to Him they will be returned" (al-An'am 6:36). The scholars whose opinion counts have agreed that what is meant by the dead in His saying, "As for the dead, Allah will raise them," is the disbelievers. The contrast in His saying, "As for the dead, Allah will raise them," with those who hear in His saying, "Only those who hear respond," supports this. What clarifies this is His saying before it: "And if their aversion is great to you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign—" (al-An'am 6:35), i.e., then do it. Then He said: "And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance, so do not be among the ignorant. Only those who hear respond..." (al-An'am 6:35–36). This is clear regarding what we have mentioned. Had what is meant by the dead been those whose souls had departed their bodies, He would have contrasted the dead with what suits them, such as saying, "Only the living respond," i.e., those whose souls have not departed their bodies. And like His saying, exalted is He: "Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one whose likeness is in darknesses from which he does not emerge? Thus has been made attractive to the disbelievers what they used to do" (al-An'am 6:122).

(p-126) So His saying in this noble verse, "Is one who was dead," i.e., a disbeliever, "and We gave him life," i.e., through faith and guidance. This is not disputed, and in it the word "death" is used to mean disbelief without any disagreement. Likewise His saying: "That he may warn whoever is living and the word may take effect against the disbelievers" (Ya-Sin 36:70). And His saying, exalted is He: "Nor are the living and the dead alike" (Fatir 35:22), i.e., the believers and the disbelievers are not alike.

Among the clearest proofs of this meaning is that His saying, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear," and the whole verse and what is in its sense of verses, is a consolation for him ﷺ, because their disbelief and their not believing grieve him, as Allah has explained in many verses:

• Such as His saying, exalted is He: "We certainly know that what they say grieves you" (al-An'am 6:33).
• And His saying, exalted is He: "And We certainly know that your breast is constricted by what they say" (al-Hijr 15:97).
• And His saying: "And do not grieve over them" (al-Nahl 16:127).
• And His saying, exalted is He: "So do not grieve over the disbelieving people" (al-Ma'idah 5:68).
• And His saying, exalted is He: "So let not your soul go out in pursuit of them in regret" (Fatir 35:8).
• And His saying, exalted is He: "Then perhaps you will kill yourself with grief over their traces if they do not believe in this message" (al-Kahf 18:6).
• And His saying, exalted is He: "Perhaps you would kill yourself that they will not be believers" (al-Shu'ara' 26:3).

And other verses beyond these, as has already been clarified. Since their disbelief and their not believing grieved him, Allah revealed many verses as a consolation for him ﷺ, in which He made clear to him that he has no power over the guidance of whomever Allah has led astray, for guidance and misguidance are in the hand of Him alone, exalted is He. He also made clear to him that he is a warner, and he has done what is incumbent upon him, warning them in the most complete and eloquent manner, and that their guidance and their misguidance are in the hand of the One who created them.

Among the verses revealed as a consolation for him ﷺ is His saying here, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear," i.e., you cannot make hear with the hearing of guidance and acceptance those whom Allah has led astray, "You can make none hear except those who believe in Our signs," meaning: you do not make hear with the hearing of guidance and acceptance except those whom We have guided to believe in Our signs, so they are Muslims.

The verses indicating this meaning are many:

• Such as His saying, exalted is He: "If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide one who misguides" (al-Nahl 16:37).
• And His saying, exalted is He: "And whoever Allah intends to test, you will not avail him anything against Allah. Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not intend to purify; for them is disgrace in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment" (al-Ma'idah 5:41).
• And His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills" (al-Qasas 28:56).
• And His saying, exalted is He: "Will you then compel the people until they become believers? And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah, and He places defilement upon those who do not reason" (Yunus 10:99–100).

And other verses beyond these (p-127). If the meaning of the verse and what resembles it, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear," i.e., those whose souls have departed their bodies, were the intended meaning, then there would be no consolation for him ﷺ in it, as you see.

Know that the verse of "al-Naml" has two other verses with its meaning. The first of them is His saying in Surah "al-Rum": "So indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs and flee. Nor can you guide the blind away from their error. You can make none hear except those who believe in Our signs, so they are Muslims" (al-Rum 30:52–53). The wording of this verse of "al-Rum" is like the wording of the verse of "al-Naml" that we are dealing with, so what we mentioned concerning the verse of "al-Naml" suffices for explaining the verse of "al-Rum."

The second of them is His saying in Surah "Fatir": "Indeed, Allah makes hear whom He wills, and you are not one to make hear those who are in the graves" (Fatir 35:22). The verse of "Fatir" is like the verses of "al-Naml" and "al-Rum" mentioned earlier, because what is meant by His saying in it, "those who are in the graves," is the dead. There is no difference between His saying, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear," and His saying, "And you are not one to make hear those who are in the graves," because what is meant by "the dead" and "those who are in the graves" is one and the same, like His saying: "And that Allah will raise those who are in the graves" (al-Hajj 22:7), i.e., He will raise all the dead, both those buried and those not buried. Qur'anic indications have also shown that the meaning of this verse of "Fatir" is like the meaning of the verse of "al-Rum." Among them is His saying before it: "You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and establish prayer" (Fatir 35:18), because its meaning is: your warning benefits only those whom Allah has guided and enabled, so that they become among those who fear their Lord unseen and establish prayer. "And you are not one to make hear those who are in the graves," i.e., the dead, i.e., the disbelievers whose wretchedness has preceded, as previously mentioned. Among them is also His saying: "Nor are the blind and the seeing alike" (Fatir 35:19), i.e., the believer and the disbeliever. And His saying after it: "Nor are the living and the dead alike" (Fatir 35:22), i.e., the believers and the disbelievers. Among them is His saying after it: "You are only a warner" (al-Tur 52:23), i.e., guidance and misguidance are not in your hand; you are only a warner, i.e., you have delivered.

The second interpretation: the dead meant are those who have actually died, but the hearing negated in His saying, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear," is specifically the customary hearing by which its possessor benefits, and this is a parable struck for the disbelievers. The disbelievers hear the sound, but they do not hear with the hearing of acceptance, with understanding and following, as He said: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and cry" (al-Baqarah 2:171). Thus the dead who are struck as a parable for it need not have all kinds of hearing negated from them, just as that was not negated from the disbelievers. Rather, the customary hearing by which they would benefit has been negated from them, but another kind of hearing has not. This second interpretation was affirmed and confined to by Abu al-Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah, as will be clarified, if Allah wills, in this discussion.

This last interpretation is also indicated by verses of the Book of Allah in which deafness, muteness and blindness are explicitly attributed to a people who speak, hear and see. What is meant by their deafness is their deafness to hearing what benefits them only, while they hear other things; likewise with sight and speech. An example is His saying, exalted is He, concerning the hypocrites: "Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return" (al-Baqarah 2:18). He described them as deaf and dumb together with the intensity of their eloquence and the sweetness of their tongues, as He stated in His saying about them: "And if they speak, you listen to what they say" (al-Munafiqun 63:4), i.e., because of their eloquence, and His saying: "Then when fear departs, they will assail you with sharp tongues" (al-Ahzab 33:19). These who, if they speak, you listen to what they say, and when fear departs, assail the Muslims with sharp tongues, are the very ones of whom Allah said: "Deaf, dumb, blind." This is only because their deafness, dumbness and blindness are with respect to one specific thing, which is what benefits from the truth. This alone is what they are deaf to, so they do not hear it, dumb to it, so they do not speak it, and blind to it, so they do not see it, though they hear other things, see them and speak them, as He said: "And We made for them hearing and sight and hearts, but their hearing and their sight and their hearts availed them nothing at all" (al-Ahqaf 46:26). This is clear, as you see.

We have clarified this to the utmost clarity, together with its Arabic evidences, in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" in Surah "al-Baqarah," in the discussion on the way of reconciling His saying about the hypocrites, "Deaf, dumb, blind" (al-Baqarah 2:18), with His saying about them: "And had Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight" (al-Baqarah 2:20);

• and His saying about them: "They assail you with sharp tongues" (al-Ahzab 33:19);
• and His saying about them also: "And if they speak, you listen to what they say" (al-Munafiqun 63:4).

We clarified there that the Arabs use deafness and absence of hearing to refer to hearing that has no benefit in it, and we mentioned some Arabic evidences for that.
