A question related to this noble verse.

Know that what the evidence requires as the more probable view is that the dead in their graves hear the speech of those who speak to them, and that the statement of 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and those who followed her, that they do not hear, based on His saying, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear," and what came in its meaning of verses, is an error on her part, may Allah be pleased with her, and on the part of those who followed her.

The explanation that the evidence requires this preference is built on two premises:

The first: that the hearing of the dead is established from the Prophet ﷺ in multiple hadiths with an established soundness free from any flaw, and he ﷺ did not state that this is specific to a particular person or to a particular time.

The Second Premise: that the authentic reports from the Prophet ﷺ concerning the hearing of the dead are not contradicted by anything established in the Book or the Sunnah. The interpretation by ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) of some verses in a sense that contradicts the aforementioned hadiths does not oblige one to adopt it, because another meaning of the verses is more correct than hers. Therefore the authentic texts from the Prophet ﷺ are not rejected on account of some Companions' interpretation of some verses. We shall clarify here, if Allah wills, the soundness of the two aforementioned premises. When it is established by this that the hearing of the dead is affirmed from him ﷺ without any explicit contrary evidence, it becomes known that the preponderance of what we have mentioned is what the evidence requires.

As for the First Premise, which is the affirmation of the hearing of the dead from the Prophet ﷺ: al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "ʿAbdullah ibn Muhammad related to me, he heard Rawh ibn ʿUbadah, who said: Saʿid ibn Abi ʿArubah related to us from Qatadah, who said: Anas ibn Malik related to us from Abu Talhah that the Prophet of Allah ﷺ ordered, on the day of Badr, twenty-four men from the chieftains of Quraysh, and they were thrown into a pit among the pits of Badr, a foul and fouling pit. And whenever he gained victory over a people, he would remain in the open ground for three nights. When he was at Badr on the third day, he ordered his mount to be saddled, and its saddle was fastened on it. Then he walked, and his companions followed him, saying: 'We think he is only going for some need,' until he stood at the edge of the well and began calling them by their names and their fathers' names: 'O so-and-so son of so-and-so, and O so-and-so son of so-and-so, would it please you that you had obeyed Allah and His Messenger? For we have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?' He said: Then ʿUmar said: 'O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, how do you speak to bodies that have no spirits?!' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, you are not more able to hear what I say than they are.'" Qatadah said: "Allah brought them back to life for him so that he could make them hear, as a rebuke, a humiliation, a punishment, a regret and a remorse." End of quotation from Sahih al-Bukhari.

So this authentic hadith is one in which the Prophet ﷺ swore that the living who were present are not more able to hear what he says than those dead people after three days. It is an authentic and explicit text on the hearing of the dead, and he ﷺ did not mention any restriction in it (p-130). The statement of Qatadah which al-Bukhari reported from him is, as far as appears, his own ijtihad (independent reasoning).

Al-Bukhari also said in his Sahih: "ʿUthman related to me, ʿAbdah related to me from Hisham from his father, from Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with both of them), who said: 'The Prophet ﷺ stopped at the well of Badr and said: "Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" Then he said: "Indeed they now hear what I say."' It was mentioned to ʿAʾishah, and she said: 'The Prophet ﷺ only said: "Indeed they now know that what I used to tell them is the truth."' Then she recited: ﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear﴾, until she recited the verse." End of quotation from Sahih al-Bukhari.

I have seen that he also related, from two noble Companions, Ibn ʿUmar and Abu Talhah, the Prophet's ﷺ explicit statement that those dead people hear what he says to them. ʿĀʾishah's rejection of the narration of Ibn ʿUmar by what she understood from the Qur'an is rejected, as you will see its explanation, if Allah the Exalted wills.

We have already clarified in the surah of "Banu Isra'il," in the discussion on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Isra': 15], that her rejection of Ibn ʿUmar's narration from the Prophet ﷺ that "the deceased is punished for the weeping of his family" by what she understood from the verse is also rejected, and we clarified that the truth lies with Ibn ʿUmar in his narration, not with her in what she understood from the Qur'an.

Al-Bukhari also said in his Sahih: "ʿAyyash related to us, ʿAbd al-Aʿla related to us, Saʿid related to us, he said: Khalifah said to me: Ibn Zurayʿ related to us, Saʿid related to us, from Qatadah, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: 'Indeed the servant, when he is placed in his grave and his companions turn away from him, and he indeed hears the sound of their sandals, two angels come to him and make him sit, and they say: What did you used to say about this man, Muhammad ﷺ? He says: I bear witness that he is the servant of Allah and His Messenger. It is said: Look at your seat in the Fire; Allah has replaced it for you with a seat in Paradise.'" The hadith... I have seen in this authentic hadith the Prophet's ﷺ explicit statement that the dead person in his grave hears the sound of the sandals of those who buried him when they return, and it is an authentic and explicit text on the hearing of the dead, and he ﷺ did not mention any restriction in it.

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his Sahih: "Ishaq ibn ʿUmar ibn Salit al-Hudhali related to me, Sulayman ibn al-Mughirah related to us, from Thabit, who said: Anas said: I was with ʿUmar [ḥ], and Shaybān ibn Farrukh related to us, and the wording is his: Sulayman ibn al-Mughirah ibn Thabit related to us, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: We were with ʿUmar between Makkah and Madinah when we sighted the crescent..." The hadith; and in it: He said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to show us the places of fall of the people of Badr" yesterday, saying: "This is the place of the fall of so-and-so tomorrow, if Allah wills." He said: ʿUmar said: "By Him who sent him with the truth, they did not overstep the limits which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had set, and they were thrown into a well, one upon another." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went until he reached them and said: "O so-and-so son of so-and-so, and O so-and-so son of so-and-so, have you found what Allah and His Messenger promised you to be true? For I have found what Allah promised me to be true." ʿUmar said: "O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, how do you speak to bodies that have no spirits in them?" He said: "You are not more able to hear what I say than they are, except that they cannot answer me in anything."

Hadith: Harram ibn Khalid related to us, Hammad ibn Salamah related to us from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ left the slain of Badr for three days, then came to them, stood over them and called to them, saying: 'O Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, O Umayyah ibn Khalaf, O ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, O Shaybah ibn Rabiʿah, have you not found what Allah promised you to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true.' ʿUmar heard the words of the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how can they hear, and how can they answer, when they have decayed?' He said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, you are not more able to hear what I say than they are, but they cannot answer.' Then he ordered them to be dragged and they were cast into the well of Badr."

Then Muslim mentioned after this the narration of Anas from Abu Talhah which we related from al-Bukhari. So you see these hadiths established in the Sahih from ʿUmar and his son, Anas, and Abu Talhah (may Allah be pleased with them), in which there is an explicit statement from the Prophet ﷺ that the living who were present are not more able to hear than those dead people what he ﷺ says. He ﷺ swore to this and did not mention any restriction. Muslim (may Allah have mercy on him) also said in his Sahih: "ʿAbd ibn Humayd related to us, Yunus ibn Muhammad related to us, Shaybān ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman related to us, from Qatadah, Anas ibn Malik related to us, who said: The Prophet of Allah ﷺ said: 'Indeed the servant, when he is placed in his grave and his companions turn away from him, indeed he hears the sound of their sandals.' He said: 'Two angels come to him and make him sit...'" The hadith; and in it is the Prophet's ﷺ explicit statement of the deceased's hearing of the sound of sandals in his grave. It is an authentic and explicit text on the hearing of the dead, and its apparent meaning is general for everyone buried whose people have turned away from him, as you see.

Among the hadiths indicating the generality of the hearing of the dead is what Muslim related in his Sahih: "Yahya ibn Yahya al-Tamimi, Yahya ibn Ayyub, and Qutaybah ibn Saʿid related to us; Yahya ibn Yahya said: 'He informed us,' and the other two said: 'Isma'il ibn Ja'far related to us from Sharik, who is Ibn Abi Namir, from ʿAta' ibn Yasar, from ʿAʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her), that she said: 'Whenever it was her night with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would go out at the end of the night to al-Baqiʿ, and say: "Peace be upon you, abode of a believing people; what you were promised comes to you tomorrow, deferred; and indeed we, if Allah wills, will join you. O Allah, forgive the people of the Baqiʿ al-Gharqad."' Qutaybah did not include his words: "What you are promised comes to you."'" In another narration in Sahih Muslim from her, she said: "How should I say to them, O Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" He said: "Say: Peace be upon the people of the abodes among the believers and the Muslims, and may Allah have mercy on those who went before us and those who come after, and indeed we, if Allah wills, will join you."

Then Muslim (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah and Zuhayr ibn Harb related to us, both said: Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Asadi related to us from Sufyan, from ʿAlqamah ibn Martad, from Sulayman ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to teach them, when they went out to the graveyards, that the speaker among them would say, in the narration of Abu Bakr: 'Peace be upon the people of the abodes,' and in the narration of Zuhayr: 'Peace be upon you, people of the abodes, among the believers and the Muslims; and indeed we, if Allah wills, will join you. We ask Allah for well-being for us and for you.'" End of quotation from Sahih Muslim.

His ﷺ address to the people of the graves with his words "Peace be upon you," and his saying "and indeed we, if Allah wills, will join you," and the like, clearly indicates that they hear his greeting, because if they did not hear his greeting and speech, his address to them would be of the same kind as addressing the non-existent, and there is no doubt that this is not the way of sensible people; so it is very far-fetched that it issues from him ﷺ. The hadith of ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs will come, if Allah wills, indicating that the dead person in his grave is comforted by the presence of the living beside him.

When you have seen these authentic proofs indicating the hearing of the dead, know that the Qur'anic verses, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear﴾, and His saying: ﴿And you are not one who can make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir: 22], do not contradict them. We have clarified the sound of the aspects of their interpretation, mentioned the indication of the Qur'anic contextual clues upon it, and that the induction (istiqra') of the Qur'an indicates it.

Among those who affirmed definitively that the aforementioned verses do not conflict with the authentic hadiths we have mentioned is Abu al-ʿAbbas Ibn Taymiyyah. He said in the fourth volume of "Majmu' al-Fatawa," from page 295 to page 299, the following text: "The spirit may be returned to the body at times other than the time of questioning, as in the hadith which Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr graded as sound from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: 'There is no man who passes by the grave of a man whom he knew in the world, and greets him, except that Allah returns his spirit to him until he returns his greeting.'" In the Sunan of Abu Dawud and others, from Aws ibn Abi Aws al-Thaqafi, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Indeed the best of your days is Friday, so increase your blessings upon me on Friday and the night of Friday, for your blessings are presented to me." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how will our blessings be presented to you when you have decayed?" He said: "Indeed Allah has forbidden the earth to consume the bodies of the prophets." This chapter contains hadiths and reports, more than this time can cover, which show that the bodies in the graves experience bliss and punishment if Allah wills that, as He wills, and that the spirits remain after separation from the body, either blessed or punished. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ commanded the greeting of the dead, as is established in the Sahih and Sunan that he used to teach (p-133) his companions, when they visited the graves, to say: "Peace be upon you, people of the abodes, among the believers, and indeed we, if Allah wills, will join you. May Allah have mercy on those who went before us and those who came after, from us and from you. We ask Allah for well-being for us and for you. O Allah, do not deprive us of their reward, nor tempt us after them, and forgive us and them." Indeed, this has been revealed to many people, so that they heard the voices of the punished in their graves and saw them with their own eyes being punished in their graves, in many well-known reports. But it is not necessary that this should always be upon the body at every time; rather, it is permissible that it be in a state.

[p. 133]

It is narrated in the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn, the two most authentic collections of hadith, al-Bukhari and Muslim) from Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ left the slain of Badr for three days, then came to them, stood over them, and said: "O Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, O Umayyah ibn Khalaf, O Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, O Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, have you not found what your Lord promised you to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, heard the words of the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can they hear, when they have decayed?" He said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, you are not more able to hear what I say than they are, but they cannot answer." Then he ordered them, and they were dragged and thrown into the well of Badr.

It is also narrated in the two Sahihs from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "the Prophet ﷺ stood over the well of Badr and said: 'Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?' And he said: 'Indeed they now hear what I say.'" This was mentioned to Aisha, and she said: "Ibn Umar made a mistake. What the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said was: 'Indeed they now know that what I told them is the truth.'" Then she recited the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾, and she recited the verse to its end.

The scholars of hadith agree on the soundness of what was related by Anas and Ibn Umar, even though neither of them witnessed Badr. Anas related it from Abu Talhah, and Abu Talhah did witness Badr, as Abu Hatim recorded in his Sahih from Anas, from Abu Talhah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ "commanded on the day of Badr concerning twenty-four men from the leaders of Quraysh, and they were thrown into a pit of Badr called Tawi. When he prevailed over a people, he would love to stay in their courtyard for three nights. When the third day came, he ordered his riding beast to be saddled, then he set off, and his companions followed him, saying: 'We do not think he is going except for some need,' until he stood at the edge of the well and began calling to them by their names and the names of their fathers: 'O so-and-so son of so-and-so, would it please you that you had obeyed Allah and His Messenger? For we have found what our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?'" Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are speaking to bodies with no spirits in them." The Prophet ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, you are not more able to hear what I say than they are." Qatadah said: "Allah brought them back to life so that they could hear, as reproach, belittlement, punishment, regret, and remorse." Aisha, in what she related, interpreted it as she did.

The authentic text from the Prophet ﷺ takes precedence over the interpretation of those among his companions and others who interpreted it differently. Nothing in the Qur'an negates this, for the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ only intends the ordinary hearing that benefits its possessor. This is a parable Allah struck for the disbelievers, and the disbelievers do hear the sound, but they do not hear with the hearing of acceptance, understanding, and following, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the example of those who disbelieve is like one who shouts to that which hears nothing but calling and crying﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171]. Likewise, the dead whom Allah made the example of need not have all kinds of hearing negated from them. Rather, the ordinary hearing is negated, just as it was not negated from the disbelievers, but the ordinary hearing by which they would benefit was negated from them.

As for another kind of hearing, it is not negated from them. It is established in the two Sahihs and others that the dead person hears the sound of their sandals when they turn away and leave. So this agrees with that, and how can this be rejected? This is the end of the point of discussion from the words of Abu al-Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah. You see that he clearly stated that Aisha's interpretation does not override the authentic text from the Prophet ﷺ, and that there is nothing in the Qur'an that negates the hearing established for the dead in the authentic hadiths.

When you know this, that the Qur'an contains nothing that negates the mentioned hearing, you know that it is established by the authentic text without any contradiction.

The conclusion is that Aisha's interpretation of some verses of the Qur'an does not override the authentic and explicit narrations from the Prophet ﷺ transmitted by trustworthy companions. This is reinforced by three matters:

The first is what we have just mentioned, that the narration of a trustworthy reporter is not rejected by interpretation.

The second is that when Aisha denied the narration of Ibn Umar from the Prophet ﷺ, "Indeed they now hear what I say," she said: "What he ﷺ said was: 'Indeed they now know that what I was telling them is the truth.'" So she denied hearing and negated it from them, and affirmed knowledge for them. It is known that whoever has knowledge can also have hearing, as some scholars have pointed out.

The third is what came from her that indicates her retraction of her interpretation in favor of the authentic narrations.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari: "Among the strange things is that in the Maghazi of Ibn Ishaq there is a narration by Yunus ibn Bukayr with a good chain from Aisha, like the hadith of Abu Talhah, and in it: 'You are not more able to hear what I say than they are,' and Ahmad related it with a fair (hasan) chain. If it is preserved, then she retracted her denial, because of what was established for her from the narration of these companions, since she had not witnessed the incident." End of his quote. The likelihood of her retraction is strong, because what indicates her retraction was established through two chains.

Ibn Hajar said: one of them is good (jayyid) and the other is fair (hasan). Then Ibn Hajar said: al-Isma'ili said: Aisha had such understanding, intelligence, abundance of narration, and depth in subtle knowledge that there is no more to be added. But there is no way to reject the narration of a trustworthy reporter except with a text of equal strength that indicates its abrogation, its specification, or its impossibility. End of the point of discussion from the words of Ibn Hajar.

Ibn al-Qayyim said at the beginning of Kitab al-Ruh: The first issue: whether the dead know the visits and greetings of the living or not. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "No Muslim passes by the grave of his brother whom he knew in this world and greets him, except that Allah returns his soul to him until he returns the greeting." This is an explicit text that he recognizes him in person and returns his greeting.

And in the two Sahihs from him ﷺ, through multiple routes: "He ordered the slain of Badr, and they were thrown into a well. Then he came and stood over them and called them by their names: 'O so-and-so son of so-and-so, and O so-and-so son of so-and-so, have you found what your Lord promised you to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true.'" Umar said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, you are speaking to people who have decayed." He said: "By Him who sent me with the truth, you are not more able to hear what I say than they are, but they cannot answer."

It is also established from him ﷺ that the dead person hears the sound of the footsteps of those who escort him when they leave him. The Prophet ﷺ prescribed for his community that when they greet the people of the graves, they should greet them with the greeting of one who addresses someone: "Peace be upon you, abode of believing people." This is address to one who hears and understands. Were it not so, this address would be like addressing a non-existent thing or an inanimate object. The predecessors (al-Salaf) agree on this, and reports from them have been transmitted in abundance that the dead recognize the visit of the living and rejoice in it. Abu Bakr Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Ubayd ibn Abi al-Dunya said in Kitab al-Qubur:

* *

Chapter on the dead recognizing the visits of the living.

Muhammad ibn Awn narrated to us: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Abdullah ibn Sam'an, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No man visits the grave of his brother and sits beside it, except that he is comforted by him and returns his greeting, until he stands up."

Muhammad ibn Qudamah al-Jawhari narrated to us: Ma'n ibn Isa al-Qazzaz narrated to us, Hisham ibn Sa'd informed us, Zayd ibn Aslam narrated to us, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him, who said: When a man passes by the grave of his brother whom he knows and greets him, he returns the greeting and recognizes him. And when he passes by a grave he does not know and greets it, it returns the greeting.

Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned in the words of Abu al-Dunya and others narrations that imply the hearing of the dead and their recognition of those who visit them, and he mentioned in this many very numerous reports. Then he said: These reports, although by themselves they are not sufficient to establish such a matter, are, in their abundance, which none can count except Allah, in agreement on this meaning. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I see your dreams agree that they are in the last ten (nights)," meaning the Night of Power. So when the dreams of believers agree on something, it is like the agreement of their narrations about it. Among what Ibn al-Qayyim said in his lengthy words mentioned above, and it is established in the Sahih that the dead person is comforted by those who attend his funeral after his burial: Muslim related in his Sahih from the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Shamasah al-Mahri, who said: "We were present with Amr ibn al-As while he was in the throes of death, and he wept for a long time and turned his face to the wall..." The hadith continues, and in it: "When I die, do not accompany me with a wailing woman or fire. When you bury me, pour the earth over me gently, then stay around my grave for as long as it takes to slaughter a camel and divide its meat, so that I may be comforted by you and see what answer I can give to the messengers of my Lord." This indicates that the dead person is comforted by those present at his grave and is gladdened by them. End of quote.

It is known that this hadith has the ruling of a marfu' report (one traced back to the Prophet ﷺ), because the grave-dweller's comfort in the presence of the living at his grave is not an area where personal opinion has any place.

Among what Ibn al-Qayyim said in his lengthy words mentioned above: It suffices in this that the Muslim who greets them is called a visitor, and were they not aware of him, it would not be correct to call him a visitor, for if the one visited does not know of the visitor's visit, it is not correct to say he visited him. This is what is understood from visiting by all nations. Likewise the greeting of them, for greeting one who is not aware of and does not know the Muslim is impossible. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community that when they visit graves they should say: "Peace be upon you, people of these abodes, from among the believers and the Muslims, and we, if Allah wills, will be joining you. May Allah have mercy on those of us who went before and those who come after. We ask Allah for well-being for us and for you." This greeting, address, and calling is directed to one who hears, addresses, understands, and responds, even if the Muslim does not hear the response.

Among what Ibn al-Qayyim said in his lengthy words is his statement: The hafiz Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq al-Ishbili included a chapter on this, saying: "Mention of what has come that the dead are asked about the living, and they know their sayings and deeds." Then he said: Abu Umar Ibn Abd al-Barr related from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ: "No man passes by the grave of his believing brother whom he knew and greets him, except that he recognizes him and returns his greeting."

It is also narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, as a marfu' report, who said: "If he does not recognize him and greets him, he returns his greeting." He said: It is also narrated from the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No man visits the grave of his brother and sits beside it, except that he is comforted by him until he stands up." The hafiz Abu Muhammad argued on this point with what Abu Dawud related in his Sunan from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No one greets me except that Allah returns my soul to me until I return his greeting."

Then Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned from Abd al-Haqq and others reports and narrations on the subject. Then he said in his lengthy words: This is also indicated by the practice of people from ancient times until now of giving instruction (talqin) to the dead in his grave. Were it not that he hears this and benefits from it, there would be no benefit in it, and it would be pointless. The Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, was asked about it, and he approved of it and argued for it by the practice.

It is narrated in this regard a weak hadith. Al-Tabarani mentioned in his Mu'jam, from the hadith of Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies and you have heaped the earth over him, let one of you stand at the head of his grave and say: O so-and-so, son of so-and-so's mother," the hadith... And in it: "Recall what you departed the world upon: the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and that you were content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, with Muhammad as prophet, and with the Qur'an as imam," the hadith...

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said: This hadith, even if it is not established, the continuous practice of it in all the regions and all the eras without denial is sufficient for acting upon it. Allah, glory be to Him, has never let custom run such that a nation spread across the eastern and western lands, and it is the most complete of nations in intellect and the most abundant in knowledge, agrees upon addressing one who does not hear, and considers that good, with none of them denying it; rather the first set it as a sunnah for the last, and the last follow the first in it. Had the address not been heard, that would be like addressing dust, wood, stone and non-existence. And this, even if one person considered it good, the scholars as a whole are agreed on its being disapproved and deemed repugnant.

Abu Dawud related in his Sunan, with a chain that is not objectionable: that the Prophet (ﷺ) attended the funeral of a man, and when he had been buried he said: "Ask for steadfastness for your brother, for he is now being questioned." Thus he informed that he is questioned at that time, and if he is questioned, then he hears the prompting. And it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "the deceased hears the sound of their sandals when they turn and leave."

Then Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned the story of al-Sa'b ibn Jaththamah and 'Awf ibn Malik, and 'Awf's carrying out of al-Sa'b's bequest to him in a dream after his death, and he praised 'Awf ibn Malik for his understanding in carrying out the bequest of al-Sa'b after his death, since the correctness of that was known by the indications. The bequest that 'Awf carried out included giving ten dinars to a Jew from al-Sa'b's estate, which was a debt owed to him, and al-Sa'b died before it was settled.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: This is from the understanding of 'Awf ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, and he was one of the Companions, in that he carried out the bequest of al-Sa'b ibn Jaththamah after his death, and he knew the correctness of his statement by the indications he was informed of: that the dinars were ten and were in the horn; then he asked the Jew and his statement matched what was in the vision, so 'Awf was certain of the correctness of the matter, and gave the Jew the dinars. This is an understanding that befits only the most learned of people in jurisprudence, namely the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Most of the later scholars probably deny this and say: How was it permissible for 'Awf to transfer the dinars from the estate of a deceased man, which belonged to his orphans and heirs, to a Jew on the basis of a dream?

Then Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned the carrying out by Khalid and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with them both, of the bequest of Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, may Allah be pleased with him, after his death. In his aforementioned bequest was the settlement of a debt which he specified to a man in a dream, and the freeing of some of his slaves. He described to the man who saw him in his dream the place where the man who stole his armour had put it, and they found the matter as he said. His story is well known.

Since the bequest of the deceased after his death has been carried out in some instances by the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that indicates that he perceives, understands and hears. Then Ibn al-Qayyim said at the conclusion of his lengthy discourse: The purpose is the answer to the questioner, and that when the deceased knows such particulars and their details, then his knowledge of the living visiting him, greeting him and supplicating for him is more fitting and more deserving. End quote.

So this lengthy discourse of Ibn al-Qayyim, of which we have quoted part in summary and part in detail, contains convincing proofs sufficient to indicate that the dead hear. Likewise is the statement we quoted from his teacher Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah, and in their statements that we quoted from them are authentic hadiths, many reports, widespread visions, and other things. It is known that what we mentioned in Ibn al-Qayyim's words about prompting the deceased after burial was denied by some scholars, who said it is an innovation and that there is no evidence for it, and this was reported from Imam Ahmad, that he did not act upon it except the people of Syria. You have seen that Ibn al-Qayyim argued for it with proofs, among them: that Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, was asked about it and he deemed it good, and he argued for it by practice. Among them: that the practice of the Muslims has continued with it in all the regions and eras without denial.

And among them: that the deceased hears the sound of the sandals of those burying him when they turn and leave. His use of this authentic hadith as evidence is a very strong argument, because if at that time he hears the sound of sandals, then hearing clear speech in the form of prompting from the owners of the sandals is more fitting and more deserving. His use of the hadith of Abu Dawud, "Ask for steadfastness for your brother, for he is now being questioned," for this has a basis in reasoning, because if he hears the questioner's question, then he hears the prompter's prompting. And Allah knows best.

The distinction between his hearing the questioning of the angel and his hearing the prompting from the burying people is a strong possibility. As for what some have mentioned, that prompting after death was done only by the people of Syria, it is said in reply: they were the first to do it, but people followed them in that, as is known among the Malikis and Shafi'is. Shaykh al-Hattab said in his commentary on the words of Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Maliki in his Mukhtasar: "and prompting him the testimony," and al-Nawawi affirmed the recommendation of prompting after burial.

Shaykh Zarruq said in his commentary on al-Risalah and al-Irshad, when Abu Bakr ibn al-Tula' of the Malikis was asked about it: "It is what we choose and act upon, and we have transmitted a hadith about it from Abu Umamah that is not strong, but it is supported by corroborations and the practice of the people of Syria in former times." Until he said: And he said in al-Madkhal: It is fitting that whoever is among the people of virtue and religion should check on him after the people have left him, and stand at his grave facing him and prompt him, because the two angels, peace be upon them, at that time question him, and he hears the sound of the sandals of those departing.

Abu Dawud related in his Sunan from Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished burying the dead he would stand over him and say: "Ask forgiveness for your brother and ask for him steadfastness, for he is now being questioned." Until he said: My master Abu Hamid ibn al-Baqqal, who was one of the great scholars and righteous, when he attended a funeral would offer condolences to its people after the burial and leave with those who were leaving, then he would withdraw for a little while until the people had gone, then come to the grave and remind the deceased of what he should answer the two angels, peace be upon them. End of the relevant point of al-Hattab's words.

What Abu Bakr ibn al-Tula' the Maliki said has a strong basis in reasoning, as you will see its clarification, God willing.

Then al-Hattab said: Al-Qurtubi, al-Tha'alibi and others also recommended prompting after burial, and it appears from the words of Abu ... at the beginning of the Book of Funerals, meaning from Sahih Muslim, and in the hadith of 'Amr ibn al-'As in the Book of Faith, an inclination towards it. End quote from al-Hattab. The hadith of 'Amr ibn al-'As referred to is the one whose relevant point we mentioned in the lengthy words of Ibn al-Qayyim above.

Muslim said in his Sahih: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna al-'Anazi, Abu Ma'n al-Raqashi, and Ishaq ibn Mansur related to us, all from Abu 'Asim; the wording is that of Ibn al-Muthanna: al-Dahhak, meaning Abu 'Asim, related to us, he said: Haywah ibn Shurayh informed us, he said: Yazid ibn Abi Habib related to me, from Ibn Shamasah al-Mahri, who said: We attended 'Amr ibn al-'As while he was in the throes of death, and he wept for a long time and turned his face to the wall, the hadith... We have already mentioned its relevant point in its wording in the words of Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned, and we have mentioned that this hadith of 'Amr has the ruling of being traced to the Prophet, and that it is valid evidence for the deceased finding comfort in the presence of the living at his grave.

Al-Nawawi said in "Rawdat al-Talibin," the text of which is: It is recommended that the deceased be prompted after burial, so it is said: "O servant of Allah, son of the handmaid of Allah, recall what you departed the world upon: the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and that Paradise is true, and that Hellfire is true, and that resurrection is true, and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will raise those in the graves, and you were content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, with Muhammad (ﷺ) as prophet, with the Qur'an as imam, with the Ka'bah as qiblah, and with the believers as brothers," as reported by a narration from the Prophet (ﷺ).

I say: This prompting has been recommended by a group of our companions, among them al-Qadi Husayn, the author of al-Tatimmah, Shaykh Nasr al-Maqdisi in his book "al-Tahdhib," and others, and al-Qadi Husayn transmitted it from our companions without qualification. The hadith reported concerning it is weak, but hadiths of virtues are treated with leniency among the scholars of hadith and others, and this hadith is supported by corroborations from authentic hadiths, such as the hadith: "Ask for him steadfastness," and the bequest of 'Amr ibn al-'As: "Stand by my grave for as long as it takes to slaughter a camel and divide its meat, so that I may be comforted by you and know what answer I will give the messengers of my Lord," narrated by Muslim in his Sahih. The people of Syria have continued to act upon this prompting from the earliest era and in the time of those who are followed. End of the relevant point of al-Nawawi's words.

From what Ibn al-Qayyim, Ibn al-Tula', the author of al-Madkhal among the Malikis, and al-Nawawi among the Shafi'is mentioned, as we have clarified their words, you know that prompting after burial has a strong basis in reasoning, because a weak hadith has been reported about it, it is supported by authentic corroborations, by the practice of the people of Syria in former times, and by the following of others.

And from what is known in the science of hadith of leniency in acting upon weak hadiths in matters of virtues, especially those supported by something authentic, and the clarification of how the corroborations give it support: the reality of prompting after burial is composed of two things. One: the deceased's hearing the speech of his prompter after his burial. The second: his benefiting from that prompting. Both are established in general. As for his hearing the speech of the prompter, it is supported by his hearing the sound of the prompter's sandals, established in the Two Sahihs, and hearing his speech is no farther than hearing the sound of his sandals, as you see. As for his benefiting from the prompter's speech, it is supported by his benefiting from the living person's supplication at the time of questioning in the hadith: "Ask for your brother steadfastness, for he is now being questioned," and the possibility of distinguishing between supplication and prompting is very strong, as you see. So if at the time of questioning he benefits from the speech of the living, which is his supplication for him, that supports his benefiting from the speech of the living which is his prompting him and guiding him to the answer to the two angels. In the first, all of it is hearing by the deceased of the speech of the living; in the second, it is benefit by the deceased from the speech of the living at the time of questioning. And you have known the strength of the possibility of distinguishing between supplication and prompting.

Within all of this is evidence that the dead hear the speech of the living. Among the clearest proofs for the instruction (talqin) after burial is the greeting of peace upon them, and the address to them is the address of one who hears and knows when visited, as has already been explained. For each of these is a direct address to the deceased in his grave.

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, in his commentary on Surat al-Rum, upheld the hearing of the dead in his discussion of the verse: ﴿So you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾, up to His words: ﴿and they are Muslims﴾ [al-Rum: 32-33]. He cited in this many of the evidences that we presented in the words of Ibn al-Qayyim, Ibn Abi al-Dunya and others, and many reports (maraʾi) indicating this. We have already presented the hadith indicating that reports (maraʾi), when they are widely transmitted (tawatur), establish proof.

Among what he said in the aforementioned discussion: The Mother of the Believers, ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, used this verse, ﴿So you cannot make the dead hear﴾, to refute the error (tawhim) of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, in his narration that the Prophet ﷺ addressed the slain who were thrown into the well of Badr after three days. He continued: The correct view among the scholars is the narration of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, because of the supporting evidences for its authenticity. Among the most famous of these is what Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr narrated, declaring it sound, from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (marfuʿ): «There is no one who passes by the grave of his Muslim brother whom he used to know, except that Allah returns to him his soul so that he may return his greeting» (al-hadith).

We have presented this in this discussion many times. From all that we have mentioned in this discussion, in the commentary on this verse of Surat al-Naml, you know that what the evidence supports is that the dead hear the greetings and address of the living, whether we say that Allah returns their spirits to them so that they hear the address and return the answer, or we say that the spirits also hear and respond after the bodies have perished. For we have already shown that this rests on two premises: the establishment of the hearing of the dead through authentic Sunnah, and that the Qur'an does not contradict it under the correct interpretation (p-142), which is supported by the Qur'anic indications and the inductive study of the Qur'an. When this is established by authentic Sunnah without opposition from any Book or Sunnah, its preference becomes clear over ʿAʾishah's interpretation, and that of those who followed her, of some verses of the Qur'an, as has already been explained.

In the evidences that Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned in Kitab al-Ruh regarding this there is persuasion for the fair-minded. We have added to them what you have seen. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And on the Day We gather from every nation a band of those who denied Our signs, and they will be driven in ranks﴾. The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that the gathering is specific to these bands who denied the signs of Allah. However, many verses have indicated that the gathering is general for all creation:

• such as His saying, may He be exalted, shortly after this: ﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾ [al-Naml: 87],

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We gathered them, and We left out none of them﴾ [al-Kahf: 47],

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And on the Day We gather them all﴾ [al-An'am: 22],

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you. We have not neglected in the Book anything. Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ [al-An'am: 38],

and other verses besides these.

We have clarified in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), regarding this verse of "al-Naml", the way of reconciling His saying in it: ﴿And on the Day We gather from every nation a band﴾ (the verse), with His saying: ﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾ [al-Naml: 87], and similar verses. We mentioned al-Alusi's statement in his tafsir that His saying: ﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾ refers to the general gathering of all people for reckoning and recompense. And His saying: ﴿And on the Day We gather from every nation a band﴾ refers to the specific gathering of these bands who denied, for the sake of the rebuke stated in His saying here: ﴿Until, when they arrive, He will say, "Did you deny My signs while you did not encompass them in knowledge?"﴾ (the verse) [al-Naml: 84]. The Qur'an indicates this, as you see.

Some have said: these bands that are gathered in a specific gathering are the leaders of the people of misguidance and their chiefs. Accordingly, the verse is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils, then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees﴾ ﴿Then We will surely draw out from every sect whichever of them was most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam: 68-69]. The word "fawj" (band) means a group of people. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They enter into the religion of Allah in multitudes﴾ [al-Nasr: 2]. And His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿and they will be driven in ranks﴾, meaning: the first of them comes to (p-143) the last of them until they gather, then they are all pushed on together, as said by more than one scholar.

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And on the Day We gather from every nation a band of those who denied Our signs﴾.

The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that the gathering is specific to these denying bands, and His saying shortly after: ﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾ [al-Naml: 87], indicates that the gathering is general, as the Qur'anic verses have stated many times.

The answer to this is what al-Alusi explained in his tafsir: that His saying: ﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾ means the general gathering, and His saying: ﴿And on the Day We gather from every nation a band﴾ means, after the general gathering, Allah gathers those who denied the messengers from every nation for the rebuke stated in His saying: ﴿Did you deny My signs while you did not encompass them in knowledge, or what were you doing?﴾ [al-Naml: 84]. So the intended "band from every nation" is the band that denied the messengers, gathered in a specific gathering for rebuke. This does not contradict the gathering of all for the decisive judgment. This view is better than restricting the "band" to the leaders, as some have held.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 84:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Until, when they arrive, He will say: "Did you deny My verses while you did not encompass them in knowledge? Or what was it that you were doing?"﴾. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir of this noble verse: That is, they are questioned about their belief (i'tiqad) and their deeds. The purpose of His question about their belief is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Did you deny My verses?﴾, because affirming the verses of Allah, which are this Qur'an, is among the articles of faith (aqa'id al-iman) that are indispensable, as is known from the hadith of Jibril and others. The purpose of His question about their deeds is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or what was it that you were doing?﴾. The question mentioned is a question of reproach and rebuke, for He, may He be exalted, has rebuked them in it for corrupt belief and corrupt deeds. The rebuke for both together, as mentioned here, has a parallel in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he did not believe and did not pray, but he denied and turned away﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31], as Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed out. So His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿So he did not believe﴾ and His saying ﴿but he denied﴾ are a rebuke for corrupt belief. And His saying ﴿and did not pray﴾ is a rebuke for neglecting action.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 86:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein, and the day to give sight? Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ We have already presented the clear signs concerning this in Surat "Bani Isra'il," in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, and We effaced the sign of the night﴾ [al-Isra': 12], and so on.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 88:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them rigid, while they pass by as the clouds pass. [It is] the handiwork of Allah, who perfected everything. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

We have already mentioned, in the introduction to this blessed book, that among the types of clarification (bayan) it contains is that some scholars say a statement about a verse, while the verse contains an indicator (qarinah) showing that this statement is invalid. We also mentioned in its introduction that among the types of clarification it contains is establishing a meaning by the fact that it is the predominant one in the Qur'an, since its predominance in it indicates that it has not departed from the meaning of the verse. We gave many examples of all of this in this blessed book, and both of the aforementioned types of clarification are combined in this verse of "An-Naml."

The explanation of this is that some people have claimed that His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them rigid, while they pass by as the clouds pass﴾, indicates that the mountains, in the present worldly life, are thought by the beholder to be rigid, i.e., standing still and motionless, while they are passing by as the clouds pass. Similar to this is the saying of An-Nabigha describing an army:

"With a host like a mountain, you think that they
are standing for a pilgrim while the riding-camels are trotting."

The two aforementioned types of clarification show the invalidity of this statement.

(p-145) As for the first of them, namely the presence of an indicator showing its invalidity: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And you see the mountains﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to His saying "fa-fazi'a" (then were terrified), and that conjoined element is ordered with the particle "fa" after His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And [mention] the Day the Horn is blown, and those in the heavens and those on the earth are terrified﴾ up to the verse [an-Naml: 87], i.e., "And the Day the Horn is blown, so those in the heavens are terrified, and you see the mountains." This clear Qur'anic indicator shows that the passing of the mountains as the clouds pass occurs on the Day the Horn is blown, not now.

As for the second, namely that this meaning is the predominant one in the Qur'an, it is clear, since all the verses in which the movement of the mountains appears are on the Day of Resurrection:

• such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day when the sky will sway violently and the mountains will move swiftly﴾ [at-Tur: 9-10],

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Day We will set the mountains in motion, and you will see the earth emerging﴾ [al-Kahf: 47],

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾ [an-Naba': 20],

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the mountains are set in motion﴾ [at-Takwir: 3].

As for His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿the handiwork of Allah, who perfected everything﴾, its like has come in many verses, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no inconsistency﴾ [al-Mulk: 3]. The setting in motion of the mountains, their creation, and their erection before being set in motion are all a perfected handiwork.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿Indeed, He is Acquainted with what you do﴾, we have already mentioned the verses with this meaning at the beginning of Surah Hud, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold their chests to hide from Him﴾, up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of the contents of the breasts﴾ [Hud: 5].

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them rigid, while they pass by as the clouds pass.﴾

(p-360) This verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates that the mountains are thought by the beholder to be still while they are moving. Other verses have come indicating that the mountains are firmly set, and the firmly set (rasi) is that which is fixed in a place, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the mountains He has set firmly﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 32], and His saying: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you﴾ [an-Nahl: 15].

And His saying: ﴿And the earth We have spread out and cast into it firm mountains﴾ [al-Hijr: 19], and His saying: ﴿And We placed within it firmly set mountains, towering high﴾ [al-Mursalat: 27].

The manner of reconciling these is evident: His saying "arsaha" (He has set it firmly) and similar expressions refer to the worldly life, while His saying ﴿and it passes by as the clouds pass﴾ refers to the Hereafter, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And [mention] the Day the Horn is blown, and those in the heavens are terrified﴾ [an-Naml: 87], then He conjoined to that His saying: ﴿And you see the mountains﴾, up to the verse.

Among what indicates this are the Qur'anic texts that the movement of the mountains is on the Day of Resurrection, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Day We will set the mountains in motion, and you will see the earth emerging﴾ [al-Kahf: 47], and His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾ [an-Naba': 20].

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 89:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him there is better than it﴾. Know that the "good deed" (ḥasanah) in this noble verse includes two kinds of good deeds:

The first: a good deed is an act of goodness performed by the servant, such as spending in the way of Allah, giving one's self and wealth to raise the word of Allah, and the like. The meaning of His saying, ﴿for him there is better than it﴾, with regard to this kind of good deed, is that the reward is multiplied, so it is better than the deed itself. For whoever spends one dirham in the way of Allah, and Allah gives him a reward of seven hundred dirhams, then he has with Allah a reward of seven hundred dirhams, for example, which is better than the good deed he sent forward, which is the spending of one dirham. There is no difficulty in this, as you can see.

(p-146) This meaning is clarified by verses of the Book of Allah, such as His saying, ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him are ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160]. It is known that ten times the good deed is better than it alone. Also His saying, ﴿And if it is a good deed, He doubles it﴾ [al-Nisa': 40], and His saying, ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261].

As for the second kind of good deed: it is like the saying of some of the people of knowledge (ahl al-'ilm) that the intended meaning of "good deed" in this verse is: "There is no god but Allah." Nothing is better than "There is no god but Allah." Rather, it is the foundation of all good. What appears to be the meaning according to this view is that the word "khayr" (better) is not a comparative form (ṣīghat tafḍīl, the comparative form).

The meaning is: for him there is a great good with Allah, obtained by him from it, that is, from its source and on account of it. Accordingly, the word "min" (from) in the verse is like His saying, ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned and then made to enter the Fire﴾ [Nuh: 25], meaning: because of their sins they were drowned, and then made to enter the Fire. As for the first view, "khayr" is a comparative form. In my opinion, it is also possible that the word "khayr" in the second view is a comparative form, but it does not mean that anything is preferred over "There is no god but Allah." Rather, the meaning is that the word "There is no god but Allah" is the means by which the servant worships in the abode of this world, and his worshipping by it is a pure act of his. Allah has rewarded him in the Hereafter for his worship by it, and the reward of Allah is His act, exalted is He. There is no doubt that the act of Allah is better than the act of His servant. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will be safe from the terror of that Day﴾. Its meaning is indicated by verses of the Book of Allah:

• His saying, may He be exalted, concerning their safety from terror: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Anbiya': 103].

• His saying, may He be exalted, concerning their safety: ﴿For them is the reward of double for what they did, and they will be secure in the lofty chambers﴾ [Saba': 37].

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is he who is thrown into the Fire better, or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾, to the end of the verse [Fussilat: 40].

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will be safe from terror on that Day﴾ [al-Naml: 89]. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "faz'in" with tanwīn (nunation) and with a fatḥah on the mīm of "yawma'idhin." The rest read it without tanwīn, rather in the idāfah (construct) to "yawma'idhin." However, Nāfi' read with a fatḥah on the mīm of "yawma'idhin" with "faz'" in idāfah to it. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū ʿAmr read with the idāfah of "faz'" to "yawma'idhin" with a kasrah on the mīm of "yawma'idhin," and with fatḥah and kasrah on the mīm of the like of "yawma'idhin." We have explained these dialects with their Arabic evidences, together with clarifying the preferred dialects, in surah (p-147) "Maryam," in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And peace be upon him on the day he was born, and the day he dies﴾, to the end of the verse [Maryam: 15].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever comes with an evil deed, they will be thrown on their faces into the Fire. Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, and Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with them, along with Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Abu Wa'il, Abu Salih, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Zuhri, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, that it means shirk (polytheism).

This noble verse contains two matters:

The first: whoever comes to his Lord on the Day of Resurrection with an evil deed, such as shirk, his face will be thrown down into the Fire.

The second: an evil deed is only recompensed with its like, without any increase. These two matters have been clarified in other places. As for the first of them, there is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live﴾ [Ta-Ha: 74].

As for the second, there is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever comes with an evil deed, he will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160], and His saying: ﴿And those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except for what they used to do﴾ [al-Qasas: 84], and His saying: ﴿A recompense in accordance﴾ [al-Naba': 26].

Since you know that evil deeds are not multiplied, know that an evil deed may become great, so its recompense is magnified because of the sanctity of the place, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing – We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]; or because of the sanctity of the time, as in His saying regarding the sacred months: ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36].

Verses of the Book of Allah have also indicated that the punishment is magnified because of the greatness of the person who opposes. An example is His saying, may He be exalted, concerning our Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And had We not given you firmness, you would have almost inclined to them a little. Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double in death﴾ [al-Isra': 74–75], and His saying: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44–46], (p-148) and His saying, may He be exalted, concerning his wives (ﷺ): ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality, the punishment will be doubled for her twofold﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30]. We have previously presented a portion of discussion on this matter, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double in death﴾ [al-Isra': 75], along with the explanation of that verse and the doubling of the evil deed referred to in these two verses. If the doubling is due to the greatness of the sin, so that in its greatness it becomes like two sins, then there is no difficulty. But if the doubling is of the recompense of the evil deed, then these two verses would be specifying the verses that explicitly state that an evil deed is only recompensed with its like. All of this is possible, and knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾.
